text.p: Copper and aluminium prices rose on the London Metals Exchange overnight on shortcovering and news that hidden Dutch copper stocks didn't exist.
Wheat prices rose on news India and Russia may need to import wheat while oil prices continued to slide on the Iraqi re-entry into the market and on warmer than usual weather in the United States.
Gold edged a touch higher on a slight flight to quality as the U.S. bond and stock markets slumped.
The CRB index ended down 0.47 at 240.40.

Copper and aluminium prices pushed higher on Wednesday on bouts of shortcovering and ended near the day's highs, dealers said. Three-months copper finished the afternoon kerb at $2,163, up $27, after early short covering gains met little in the way of selling.

The market's attention was focused on tight nearby dates ahead of the "third Wednesday" pricing next week. News the Dutch Bureau of Statistics admitted supplying flawed data on copper flows through Rotterdam, which cleared up the puzzle of substantial hidden stocks, was a background factor.

Aluminium also ended firmer, up $23.50 at $1,527, after a bout of shortcovering pushed up values in the afternoon. Nickel sank to $6,710, down $90 after liquidation emerged around the $6,800 level. Lead gained $7 to finish at $679 after failing to surmount the $680 level.
Zinc also notched up $4 to $1,049. But both metals encountered some forward buying. Copper also rose on Comex, with the March contract ending 0.80 cents firmer at 100.35 cents per pound.

News India may be importing wheat rather than exporting and hopes for wheat business with Russia combined with short covering to boost CBOT wheat futures to a higher close, traders said. There was talk India was seeking 500,000 tonnes of wheat but there were signals Australia would be the likely supplier.

Also an Indian newspaper said Wednesday the government was considering importing one million tonnes of wheat. Traders said the potential business with Russia was being talked about but they remained skeptical about a significant sale of U.S. wheat to that region.

Russian Agriculture Minister Viktor Khylstun said Russia would import up to three million tonnes of wheat in 1997. Wheat also found support on talk Iraq may be a wheat buyer now that it has returned to the world oil market.
Wheat closed one to 5-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with December up 5-1/2 at $3.99.

NYMEX crude and oil products futures were hit by another wave of selling ahead of the close, sending January crude down to another intraday low. "There's been some very, very aggressive fund liquidiation, particularly in the spot (crude) and we're seeing January and February heat and gas contracts getting hit," said Gerry Samuels at ARB Oil.

The January crude contract hit a low at $23.15 before recovering to $23.35 at 1452 EST, while January gasoline was down 3.61 cents a gallon at 63.25 cents. Weakness in the cash crude market has stemmed from the return of Iraqi oil, and inventory reports released late Tuesday and earlier today showing sizable builds in the products, traders said.

New York precious metals futures ended mixed Wednesday, though the sharp fall in U.S. stocks and bonds provided some support and increased the chances for a rally going into the year-end, traders said
"Precious metals opened higher and found some support from the weaker stock market, but then saw some serious dealer selling," FIMAT New York trader John Tyree said.
"Volumes were a bit better and some traders are hoping for a shortcovering rally as the year winds down, as funds take profits on the year's downtrend, but overall the tone is still anemic," he said.

COMEX February gold ended up 10 cents at $370.60, well off its session high at $372.00. Estimated total volume in gold was 28,000 lots. Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted $368.60/369.10, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $368.25, and the New York close Tuesday at $368.40/80.
